thesis: The reader is not choosing a programme. They are deciding how the next consequential decision they are responsible for will be made, and who will have to live with it. That is the right job to be done, and it sits beyond the job they arrive with (compare credentials, check the fee, find a schedule). Each of those arrival jobs is a good thing, and the site says so, because the good thing is honoured before it is put second. The right thing the site offers is concrete and evidence-backed: across FACTS.durationLong, one live business issue within the participant's own responsibility is worked, in the open, through FACTS.trainingDays training days across FACTS.liveSessions scheduled sessions, one-to-one coaching and an applied business project, until the reasoning is visible enough for others to review and act on, and the participant keeps the method. Progress is described only as what the participant does and produces during those six months; hope is a starting point, never a verdict; recognition, fee, scholarship, refund and HRD Corp facts are the Safety rung and are stated verbatim with the decision-maker and the controlling document named. The good thing is always the reader's own temptation, spoken in the reader's voice; it is never another provider, an academic MBA or a short course. The site applies the same rule to itself: six months is sized to the job, not sold as faster; the certificate documents the work and is not the point; the fee is confirmed in writing and is not the reason. Service is the top rung: the plan the participant builds is for the people who will have to act on it, and the programme team serves the reader's decision first, including the answer that this is not the right fit.

rjtbd: The working manager's right job to be done is not to obtain a credential, to find the lowest fee or to fit a course into a calendar; those are the jobs they arrive with, and each is a good thing. The right job is to make the next consequential decision they are responsible for in a way they can examine, explain and lead other people through, while remaining in the role that produced the decision. Their role has grown faster than the way they decide: the reasoning still lives in their head, it is defended in meetings rather than shown, and more people now depend on it than before. The change of experience they want is from carrying decisions privately, by instinct alone, to working them in the open with a method they can show, so that a team, a board, a client or a family business can follow the reasoning and act on it. The programme is the right thing for that job because it is built on exactly that unit of work: one live business issue within the participant's own responsibility, taken across FACTS.durationLong from problem definition to a written action plan with decisions, actions, owners and measures, reviewed by faculty and coached one-to-one, with the frameworks retained afterwards. Everything else the site offers (CMI recognition, the published fee, the scholarship process, employer-led HRD Corp funding, published dates) is evidence and safety in service of that job, and is never presented as the job itself.

hopeWithoutPromises.principle: Hope is the basis of progress, and progress is a change of experience. The site expresses hope by describing what the participant does and produces during the six months, in present-tense activity, and by treating the reader's experience as the base they build on. It never describes what happens to the reader's career, salary, title or business afterwards.
techniques: Write the after-state as an artefact the participant holds (a written action plan with owners and measures; the frameworks in the Leverage Management System) rather than a status they attain.
Use activity verbs that are true of the programme: define, test, weigh, examine, explain, write, review, keep. Avoid attainment verbs: achieve, secure, advance, unlock, transform.
Put the reader's present state first and honour it (instinct and experience carried you here), then the change (a method you can show), then the means (six days, three sessions, coaching, project).
Wherever the certificate or 'progress' appears, render CERTIFICATE_POSITIONING.professionalRelevance in the same block, so hope and the no-guarantee sentence are read together.
Treat time as a door, not a countdown: 'the next published date is a real door' is hope; 'seats are filling' is pressure and is banned.
Let the reader own the change: the guide, the fit check and the conversation exist so the reader can decide, including deciding not now or not this route.
Keep design intent as intent: 'the programme is designed to enrich how you lead' is permitted; 'you will lead with certainty' is not.
Rewrite the FORCES list from threats addressed at the reader to changes the reader wants to be capable of meeting, so the Survival rung is acknowledged without fear as the engine.
modelLines: Instinct and experience carried you here. The next decisions affect more people, and the reasoning deserves to be visible.
Six months from now, one issue you are carrying today is written down as a plan others can follow, and the way you got there stays with you.
FORCES rewrite, item 05: 'Competitors are adapting faster than you' becomes 'Competitors are adapting; the question is how you decide what to change first.'
If the timing is not right, that is a sound decision. The next published date is a real door, not a lost one.
neverWrite: future-proof, board-ready, promotion, salary, advancement, progression (as an outcome), transform your career, secure your place, next level
any sentence in which the programme is the grammatical subject of a change in the reader's career or business
undefined norms about the reader's peers (most leaders, typically, usually, often)

rightVsGood.principle: The good thing always gets in the way of the right thing, and sometimes the shortcut cuts. On this site the good thing is always the reader's own temptation, spoken in the reader's voice and honoured as good before it is put second. It is never another provider, an academic MBA, a short course or an HRD Corp-funded programme. The site applies the same discipline to its own selling points.

theFourGoodThings.readerVoice: I want letters after my name and a certificate I can show.
theFourGoodThings.whyItIsGood: A recognised certificate is useful and can be listed on a professional profile.
theFourGoodThings.whyItComesSecond: A certificate documents work; it is not the work. If the reasoning behind your decisions does not change, the paper changes nothing for the people who depend on you.
theFourGoodThings.modelLine: The CERTIFICATE_POSITIONING.credential documents the six months of work on your own business issue; the work is the point, and CERTIFICATE_POSITIONING.professionalRelevance

theFourGoodThings.readerVoice: What does it cost, and can someone else pay?
theFourGoodThings.whyItIsGood: Price and funding are fair, necessary questions, and the answers are published and confirmed in writing.
theFourGoodThings.whyItComesSecond: A fee is only worth confirming once the work is right for your responsibility. Fit first, then the fee, any scholarship award and any employer funding, each in writing.
theFourGoodThings.modelLine: Decide whether the work is right for the responsibility you carry; then confirm the fee in writing. The standard fee is FEES.standard.label. FACTS.scholarshipEligibility

theFourGoodThings.readerVoice: Six months, no thesis: that sounds like the quick one.
theFourGoodThings.whyItIsGood: Time is the scarcest thing a working manager has, and a schedule that fits the role is a real advantage.
theFourGoodThings.whyItComesSecond: Speed is not the reason the programme is six months. Six months is the time one live issue takes to go from problem to a reviewed plan while you keep working. Assessment is a written action plan for your own business, reviewed by faculty; that is presence, not absence.
theFourGoodThings.modelLine: FACTS.durationLong is sized to the job, not to the calendar: long enough for one live issue to be defined, tested against the frameworks, coached and written into a plan others can follow.

theFourGoodThings.readerVoice: Instinct has worked so far; I can keep managing by feel.
theFourGoodThings.whyItIsGood: Instinct built on experience is real capability and the base everything else stands on.
theFourGoodThings.whyItComesSecond: The role has grown and more people now depend on the decisions. Reasoning that stays in one head cannot be reviewed, delegated or defended by anyone else.
theFourGoodThings.modelLine: Instinct carried you here. The next decisions affect more people than before, and the reasoning deserves to be visible enough for others to review and act on.

theSiteOwnShortcuts: 'Complete the Executive MBA in six months' is replaced by what changes inside the six months; the duration stays as a fact, never as the hook.
'No exam, no thesis' is replaced by the presence it hides: assessment is a written action plan on your own business, reviewed by faculty.
'Fits your calendar' becomes 'give all three sessions full attention; the applied work happens in your business between them'.
'Free' appears once per surface; the space goes to the Safety facts that do more work (no payment, no application, unsubscribe anytime).
'Awarded and endorsed by CMI' never renders without the not-an-academic-degree sentence in the same viewport.
The scholarship and HRD Corp are never the reason to choose; they are confirmed in writing after fit is decided.

otherRoutes.rule: Define the comparison group (COMPARISON_SCOPE) and explain the different purpose of each route. Never rank, never imply another route is the good thing that gets in the way. The guide would rather the reader choose the right route than this programme.
otherRoutes.academicMBA: Choose an academic MBA when the job needs an academic degree: a regulated purpose, a research foundation, a credential recognised as a degree. This programme is not that. Choose this programme when the job is a decision you carry now and need to work in the open.
otherRoutes.shortCourses: A short course serves a specific skill in a short time and does that job well. This programme serves a different job: one live issue worked across six months with faculty review and coaching. Both are legitimate; they answer different questions.
otherRoutes.comparisonTableAddition: A first row named 'Built for', them: 'Earning an academic degree through academic study, assessment and research'; us: 'Working one live business issue to a faculty-reviewed action plan across FACTS.durationLong while remaining in role.'

theShortcutCuts.whereItMayBeSaid: Only about the reader's own choices and about methods: copying a benchmark instead of testing the foundations (first-principles article), fixing the symptom instead of the structure (systems thinking), shipping the idea you like instead of the one the customer hires (design thinking), buying the tool before defining the problem (AI page), and about the site's own claims.
theShortcutCuts.whereItMayNeverBeSaid: About academic MBAs, short courses, attendance-based training, HRD Corp providers, AI vendors or any named or implied provider.
theShortcutCuts.modelLine: Benchmarking is a good thing; it tells you what worked for someone else. It cuts later because it caps you at their answer. First principles asks what is true for you.

neverWrite: not a shortcut, unlike other programmes, faster than, easier than, lighter than, better than an MBA
not another attendance certificate, certificate on a shelf, not lecturers, done coasting
the ambiguity of the promise (implies others promise vaguely)

servantLeadership.principle: Real leadership is servant leadership: the leader earns the decision by serving the people it affects first. On the site this is stated as posture and practice, never as a slogan, and it is measured by whom the plan serves. It never touches the scholarship, the fee or HRD Corp approval, where any 'deserving' language would read as selection criteria.

whereItLives.hero: The descriptor 'For people whose decisions affect more than their own desk' opens the Service rung in the first viewport; the audience section extends it: the plan you build is for the people who will have to act on it.
whereItLives.curriculum: The applied project's owners and measures are how the leader makes the plan usable by others; 'Creating Value' at each level is attached to who receives it (customers, the organisation, the participant's team). M02 JTBD gloss, subject to ABC approval: 'Which customer job is the right one to serve.'
whereItLives.howItWorks: The FLOW's 'Right Questions' is named as the moment the right job is chosen: the question that serves the people affected, not the one that is quickest to answer. The Service sentence 'make the reasoning visible enough for others to review and act on' becomes the section head.
whereItLives.faculty: Each practitioner and coach is introduced by what they do for the participant's project (review the problem definition, challenge the reasoning, coach the plan), with biographies verbatim as support and confirmed by ABC before each cohort.
whereItLives.insights: Systems thinking: the leader takes responsibility for the structure instead of assigning blame, serving the people inside the system. Design thinking: begin with the person you are trying to serve; the leader deserves the decision by serving first. First principles: owning a decision so others can test it.
whereItLives.employerRoute: Sponsorship is framed as the organisation developing a manager who is responsible for a team, with every HRD Corp decision sentence verbatim and no return claim.
whereItLives.about: The coordinator's purpose sentence leads: the person who answers your questions exists to serve your decision, including the answer that the programme is not the right fit.
whereItLives.emails: Serve answers first, then ask. The acknowledgement honours the chosen preference; the nurture emails offer the one question the reader is sitting on; the day-14 email states that 'not the right fit' is a valid outcome of the conversation.
whereItLives.assistant: Before listing features, the assistant asks one situational question about the decision or responsibility the visitor is weighing, and routes to the named coordinator as service, not deflection.
whereItLives.ctaSection: The checklist leads with the posture: the team answers for the decision you named, says plainly if it is not the right fit, and you decide your next step after receiving the information.

permittedUses: The team's posture: serve clarity first, the reader decides.
The leader's plan: the leader earns the team's trust by building a plan that serves them (owners, measures, reasoning they can follow).
Design thinking: the product deserves the customer by serving the job the customer hires it for.
forbiddenUses: Any sentence on /fees, the scholarship self-check PDF, the scholarship FAQ or any scholarship sentence in any language.
Any sentence about HRD Corp approval or the approved amount.
Any implication that a participant deserves growth, funding, an award or a result for enrolling.

oneThing: One real decision you already carry, worked in the open across six months until the people who depend on it can follow the reasoning, with the method kept.

governanceRisks.risk: 'The good thing' could be read as a label for another provider's offer when the reader's temptation coincides with a real product (an academic degree, a short course, a cheaper programme).
governanceRisks.defused: The good thing is always written in the reader's voice as a motive ('I want letters after my name'), never as a product. Other routes are described as serving a different, legitimate job, with COMPARISON_SCOPE adjacent and a 'Built for' row that names both purposes without ranking. The vocabulary list bans 'the good thing' as a label for anything but the reader's own motive.

governanceRisks.risk: 'Sometimes the shortcut cuts' turned on the site's own six months could imply that other routes are the shortcut, or that this programme is the slow, serious one.
governanceRisks.defused: The site never writes 'not a shortcut'. It replaces speed cues with what the six months demand (a written plan reviewed by faculty) and describes the duration as sized to the job. 'The shortcut cuts' is said only about methods (benchmarking, fixing symptoms, buying tools first) and about the reader's own choices.

governanceRisks.risk: Right-versus-good language can slide into judging the reader ('you are choosing the wrong thing'), which governance treats as shaming.
governanceRisks.defused: Every good thing is honoured before it is put second ('fair questions, and they come second'; 'instinct carried you here'). Headlines are the reader's own questions, not diagnoses; 'owner dependence' and 'toolkit' framings are rewritten as questions about the business or the decision.

governanceRisks.risk: Hope creeping into outcome framing: 'a plan others can follow' could become 'board-approved plan'; 'the method you keep' could become 'lifelong capability'; 'recognition for work you can show' could become promotion language.
governanceRisks.defused: All after-states are artefacts and activities (a written action plan with owners and measures; frameworks retained in the LMS). CERTIFICATE_POSITIONING.professionalRelevance renders wherever the certificate or 'show' appears. The controlled term is 'applied business project or transformation plan', never 'board-approved plan'.

governanceRisks.risk: 'Deserving comes out of serving' read as scholarship selection criteria or as a hint about who deserves funding.
governanceRisks.defused: Hard rule in servantLeadership.forbiddenUses: no serving or deserving language on /fees, the scholarship self-check, any scholarship FAQ or any HRD Corp sentence, in any language. Scholarship copy is the verbatim FACTS.scholarshipEligibility sentence plus 'The scholarship is never automatic.'

governanceRisks.risk: The owner's maxim 'he is greatest who serves most' contains 'most', which the clarity audit flags as an undefined norm wherever it appears in scanned copy.
governanceRisks.defused: The maxim is not placed in scanned copy. The site paraphrases it as 'leadership is measured by whom it serves'.

governanceRisks.risk: Naming the Survival rung (pressures the reader faces) can become fear or urgency, which governance bans.
governanceRisks.defused: Pressures are stated as facts of the role and answered with structure; FORCES item 05 is rewritten so it no longer addresses the reader's inadequacy; time is always 'a real door', never a countdown; the /intakes code comment inviting urgency is to be renamed.

governanceRisks.risk: The Success rung's existing 'Career progression' intent label and the 'Progression Guide/Check' names accumulate into an implied promotion outcome across the funnel.
governanceRisks.defused: The intent is renamed to a situation ('For my own role — I am considering the programme for myself'); the guide is named 'the 2026 programme guide' everywhere (page, form, helper, email subject and body, attachment, llms.txt); the check is 'Programme fit check' in NAV, title, eyebrow and result. The 'not a prediction of career outcomes' line stays on the check.

governanceRisks.risk: The Service rung on employer pages could imply organisational outcomes or return on the levy.
governanceRisks.defused: Employer copy frames the decision as developing a manager who is responsible for a team, on an issue the business already has; HRD_CORP_CLAIM.short and .responsibility stay verbatim; no return, growth or productivity claim appears.

governanceRisks.risk: A decision-led hero beside gown-and-cap imagery, 'awarded and endorsed' and 'graduates' can imply an academic degree; the English home body currently lacks the boundary sentence.
governanceRisks.defused: The recognition block on home renders CERTIFICATE_POSITIONING.distinction and .professionalRelevance together; the hero supporting line carries the not-an-academic-degree sentence in the first viewport; the hero image alt stays plainly descriptive.

governanceRisks.risk: The two-way fit posture ('the team will say if it is not the right fit') and 'Roy Affandi answers for your decision' are service claims that must be operationally true on every channel.
governanceRisks.defused: Both lines are flagged for confirmation with Right Dots Resources before publication; if not confirmed on a channel, the line falls back to the current controlled sentence 'The programme team will answer questions about suitability, dates, fees, recognition and employer-led HRD Corp funding.'

governanceRisks.risk: New copy in nurture emails and PDFs sits outside the clarity audit's file list, so a breach there would ship unseen (as 'Most readers', 'usually', 'Typically 18–24 months' and 'EMPLOYER DECISION BRIEF' already have).
governanceRisks.defused: The proposal fixes each existing breach in its example and recommends adding src/lib/nurture-email.ts and scripts/pdf/copy/*.json to content-clarity-audit.mjs before any rewrite lands.

governanceRisks.risk: Social-rung proof (154 graduates, 17 cohorts, graduation photo) could drift into derived claims (completion rate, satisfaction) or read as endorsement.
governanceRisks.defused: Counts are attributed to ABC's company profile and dated on every update; no derived figures; client and associate lists are captioned as organisations listed by ABC.

governanceRisks.risk: Faculty framed by what they do for the participant's project could add unverifiable colour to controlled biographies.
governanceRisks.defused: Only the 'Applied role' framing is added; names, roles, focus lines and biographies stay verbatim, affiliation not employment, and ABC confirms the assigned faculty before each cohort.

governanceRisks.risk: 'Awarded and endorsed by CMI' (ABC-owned constant) sits in tension with the controlled term 'recognised against CMI Professional Standards'.
governanceRisks.defused: The proposal never alters PROGRAMME_POSITIONING_SENTENCE and always pairs it with CERTIFICATE_POSITIONING.distinction; the wording question is referred to the evidence register, not resolved in page copy.

governanceRisks.risk: Translated equivalents: 'no commitment' subjects map to the banned ZH 无需承诺; the MS CTA 'perbualan program' is banned as a non-collocation; 'right versus good' as an idiom may not survive literal translation.
governanceRisks.defused: Day-14 subject avoids 'No commitment.' in English; MS CTAs use 'sesi perbincangan program' per ms-register.md item 54; ZH scholarship lines keep 名额有限 / 须经评估 / 书面批准 and never 折扣 / 优惠 / 折扣码; right-versus-good is translated for meaning ('good reasons, and they come second') rather than as a slogan.

governanceRisks.risk: The /apply route slug and the international intent's 'applying' contradict 'an enquiry is not admission'.
governanceRisks.defused: Copy never uses 'apply' or 'application' for an enquiry; the international intent reads 'I am enquiring from outside Malaysia'; llms.txt labels the route as the programme enquiry form. Route renaming is noted as out of scope.

multilingualNotes.zh: Translate right-versus-good for meaning, not as a slogan. Scholarship sentences carry 名额有限 / 须经评估 / 书面批准 / 个别以书面确认 / 并非自动授予. Never 无需承诺, 折扣码, 同等的公信力 or mainland lexis flagged in zh-register.md.
